answers.justification: The acoustic survey found only 0.4 L/s of service-pipe leaks and the night flow stayed at 14.6 L/s (C2, E6). The combined Ashgrove+Millbrook inflow did not change (5,060 vs 5,075 m³/day, C4), so the extra 8.6 L/s is being moved into Millbrook rather than lost, and the RC model never tested other nodes (C13).

At S1 the step in night flow (E2) fits a burst, but it also fits a transfer, because it began the same morning as the Millbrook works, whose permit required supply-continuity arrangements (E3). The boundary-valve check covered only mains connections (E5, C6), and no leak had been found, so the S1 evidence cannot tell the two apart.

The PRV outlet held at 3.97–4.03 bar throughout, the setpoint was confirmed, and there were no alarms or overrides. The valve opened further, which is what it should do in response to the extra flow (E4, C1).

The method statement and diary describe an 80 mm overland hose from Ashgrove hydrant AG-417 to Millbrook hydrant ML-112, and it was still connected on 3 Oct (C5). Millbrook's night flow fell by about 8.4 L/s at 06:38 on 9 Sept, matching Ashgrove's 8.6 L/s rise at 06:40, and combined inflow stayed the same (C4, E2).

At S1 the boundary-valve checks argue against a crossing (E5, C6). However, they only covered GIS mains connections, and the same-day start of the Millbrook works, with required continuity arrangements (E3), leaves a hydrant or temporary link live but unshown.

Smart-meter household night use did not change (C7). No other DMA showed a night-flow step and the heatwave effects had passed by 13–14 Sept (C12, E2), and Fenwick Fields' design night demand is only 0.05 L/s (C3).

There is no record either way. The blank permit §7 is normal for an open permit, the diary's 'rang control' entry was written up afterwards, the control log was taken up with the Northfield burst, call recording was offline, and the duty controller has not been interviewed (C5, C8).

The cause comes first (06:38 vs 06:40 on 9 Sept), there is a mechanism (the AG-417 to ML-112 hose, C5), and the flows match (C4 mirrors E2, with the combined balance conserved). The leak rival is ruled out by the survey (C2).
The 5 Sept service came four days before the 9 Sept step, and the outlet pressure stayed at setpoint before and after (E4, C1).
The last Fenwick homes were connected on 29 Aug, not 9 Sept. Their design night demand is 0.05 L/s against an 8.6 L/s step that appeared within four minutes at 06:40 (C3, E2).

The Station Road main was recommissioned on 27 Sept but the overland link was still connected on 3 Oct (C5). Removing it targets the supported cause, and checking the meters and logger afterwards confirms the diagnosis cheaply, compared with an £84,500 possession (C14).
PM-7 caps the outlet at 4.2 bar after 4.6 bar caused 14 bursts on cast-iron mains (E4). Raising the setpoint would risk bursts, would push more water through the link, and would hide the real cause.
Whether control was informed is still unresolved (C5, C8). A non-conformance should wait until the duty controller has been interviewed.
Telling customers about the issue is reasonable and low-risk given 38 contacts (E1), but it does not resolve the cause the way A1 does.

The mass balance, timing, documented hose and recommissioned main (C4, C5, E2) are enough to commit to removing the link (A1). A1 is low-risk and reversible, and its result will itself confirm or refute the diagnosis.

ambiguousItems: S02: at S1 a burst could reasonably be called 'supported' because the obvious rivals (PRV, demand, mains boundary valves) were excluded, but the same-day Millbrook works with required continuity arrangements (E3) leave an unmapped transfer live, so 'unknown' is also defensible.
S05: at S1, 'contradicted' (going by the boundary-valve checks) and 'unknown' (the checks did not cover hydrant links) are both defensible.
S14: customer communication could be judged 'preferred' as a low-cost parallel action, or 'acceptable'.
caseProblems: Overnight pressure at Beacon Hill fell by 0.7 bar (3.7 to 3.0) from an extra 8.6 L/s at night. That is quite a large headloss for a district fed by a 300 mm trunk main, though it is plausible if the takeoff is between the inlet and Beacon Hill.
An 80 mm hose carrying about 8.6 L/s continuously on roughly a 1 bar differential is at the high end of plausible. The case also does not say whether ML-112 has a non-return valve.
C5 is worded in a way that heavily signposts the answer: the method statement spells out the hydrant-to-hydrant link, so the H3 solution depends on one document.

rulings.explanation: At S1, E4/C1 rule out the PRV, and E3/C3/C7/C12 rule out demand. E5/C6 rule out flow through the four GIS-listed mains boundary valves. That makes a leak the best-fitting explanation by elimination, so the key's 'supported' is defensible. However, E3 records works in the adjoining DMA (Millbrook) that began on 9 Sept, the same day as the 06:40 step. Those works fall under a standing condition requiring supply-continuity arrangements. E5 itself says the check covered only 'pipe connections' and 'mains connections'. At S1 there is no positive evidence of a leak: the survey had not started, and nothing had been found or located. So a careful analyst can reasonably conclude that S1 cannot separate a burst from an unmapped temporary transfer, which makes 'unknown' defensible too. This item depends on S05: whoever treats H3 as still live at S1 will also treat H1 as unknown.
rulings.fix: Add one sentence to E5 (S1): 'I also asked network control whether any temporary cross-boundary links or works cross-feeds had been agreed in Ashgrove or its neighbours; none were on record.' This fits C8 (the log has no Station Road entry and calls were not recorded) and leaves H5 unresolved, because 'no record' does not mean 'not informed'. It gives the S1 check coverage of temporary links, so the same-day coincidence has no supported mechanism, and 'supported' for H1 at S1 becomes the single defensible answer. If the case evidence cannot be changed, the alternative is to re-key S02 as 'unknown'.

rulings.explanation: E5/C6 are a careful physical check: every GIS-listed connection was found shut, with pressure differences holding across it. That counts against a crossing, which supports the key's 'contradicted'. However, E5 explicitly limits the check to pipe/mains connections, and E3 provides a mechanism the key's rationale overlooks. Works on the adjoining Millbrook DMA, under a condition requiring supply-continuity arrangements, started on the same day as the step. Supply continuity during a main isolation plausibly involves a cross-feed, so the coincidence is not 'without mechanism'. An analyst can reasonably say S1 evidence does not exclude a hydrant or temporary link, so H3 is live but unestablished ('unknown'). Both answers are defensible.
rulings.fix: Apply the same E5 addition as for S02: the technician also confirmed with network control that no temporary cross-boundary links or works cross-feeds were on record. With that, the S1 checks reach beyond the mains valves, and 'contradicted' becomes the single defensible S1 answer. C5 can then reverse it at S2 as intended. If the case evidence cannot be changed, the alternative is to re-key S05 as 'unknown' and update the authoring notes.

rulings.explanation: A4 is a letter telling customers about the problem and that a fix is being worked on. It is harmless and reasonable, since customers have been below the 2.0 bar reference level since 9 Sept (E1), so it is at least 'acceptable'. It is not among the best next actions, however. A1 is cheap and immediately available: the hose can be removed now that Millbrook has been on its own feed since 27 Sept (C5). A1 directly restores pressure, and a letter would likely arrive after the fix and does nothing to resolve the cause. 'Preferred' means among the best actions given the evidence, and once A1 is available a communication-only step does not meet that bar. 'Acceptable' is the single best-supported answer.
rulings.fix: No change required. Optionally, add a phrase to A4 such as 'instead of acting on the network this week' to make clear that it is not among the best actions.
